query: how does the Routing Transformer decide which keys each query attends to
answer:
The Routing Transformer does not use a dense, all‑to‑all attention pattern.  
Instead, each output token (the query) is **assigned to a cluster**, and it attends only to the keys that belong to the same cluster — the “cluster memberships” shown in the routing attention diagram [Source 3].  

Thus, the selection of keys for a given query is determined by the clustering step that routes tokens to one another; queries attend to the subset of keys that share their cluster label. The excerpts do not provide the exact algorithmic details of how the clustering is performed (e.g., the scoring or assignment rule), only that the routing mechanism groups tokens into clusters which define the sparse attention pattern.

This allows the model to more directly learn its absolute positional mapping. This further improves performance for both the baseline and relative transformer (Table 2 ). We compare against COCONET as it is one of the best-performing models that has also been evaluated on the 16-note grid using the canonical dataset split. To directly compare, we re-evaluated COCONET to obtain note-wise losses on the validation set 4 . For the Transformer models (abbreviated as TF), we implemented our attention mechanisms in the Tensor2Tensor framework (Vaswani et al., 2018) . We use 8 heads, and keep the query, key (att) and value hidden size (hs) fixed within a config. We tuned number of layers (L in {4,5,6}), attention hidden size (att in {256, 512}) and pointwise feedforward hidden size (ff in {512, 1024}).
